title: Recursive Digit Sum
directAnswer: The 'super digit' of a number is found by repeatedly summing its digits until one digit remains. The input is a string `n` conceptually repeated `k` times. The key insight: you never build the giant number — `superDigit(n, k) = superDigit(digitSum(n) · k)`, because summing the digits of the concatenation is just the digit-sum of one copy times k. Reduce that seed to a single digit (loop or recurse). Even better, the result is the digital root: `1 + (m − 1) mod 9` for `m > 0`. Time is O(|n|).

remember.pattern: Collapse k copies into digitSum(n)·k, then reduce to one digit (digital root)
rules: **Never materialize** the string repeated k times — `digitSum(n repeated k) = digitSum(n) · k`.
Seed the reduction with `digitSum(n) · k`, then keep summing digits until a single digit remains.
The super digit equals the **digital root**: for `m > 0`, `1 + (m − 1) mod 9` (and 0 only when m = 0).
Parse `n` as a **string** of digits — the original number can be huge (up to 10⁵ digits), so don't read it as an int.
One reduction pass after seeding is enough conceptually, but loop/recurse until `< 10` to be safe.
whenToUse: Repeated digit-sum / 'add the digits until one digit' problems
Inputs too large to hold as a native integer (digit strings)
Collapsing a k-fold repetition without expanding it
antiSignals: You need the full intermediate sums, not just the final digit → can't shortcut to digital root
Digits are weighted (not a plain sum) → the ·k and mod-9 shortcuts break
Base is not 10 → digital root uses (base − 1), adjust the modulus
n fits comfortably in 64 bits and k = 1 → just sum digits directly, no machinery
remember.takeaway: Recursive Digit Sum is a digital-root problem dressed up with a k-fold repetition. The two insights — repetition multiplies the digit-sum by k, and repeated digit-summing is the digital root `1 + (m−1) mod 9` — turn a seemingly huge computation into O(|n|) work with no big integers.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid constructing the k-times-repeated string (which could be astronomically long) by recognising digitSum(repeat) = digitSum(n)·k, and whether you know the digital-root shortcut.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Building the string `n` repeated `k` times (memory blow-up), or reading `n` as an integer when it can be up to 10⁵ digits and overflow.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the digit-sum-times-k collapse immediately, then mention the closed-form digital root `1 + (m−1) mod 9` as the O(1)-after-seed finish, and note it generalises 'casting out nines'.

problemStatement:
The **super digit** of an integer is defined recursively: if it has only one digit, that's the super digit; otherwise it is the super digit of the sum of its digits.

You are given a string `n` and an integer `k`. The number `p` is formed by **concatenating the string `n` exactly `k` times**. Return the super digit of `p`.

For example, if `n = "148"` and `k = 3`, then `p = "148148148"`. The super digit reduces `148148148 → 1+4+8+1+4+8+1+4+8 = 39 → 3+9 = 12 → 1+2 = 3`, so the answer is **3**.
constraints: 1 ≤ |n| ≤ 10⁵ (n is given as a string of digits)
p (n repeated k times) can be astronomically large — never build it
The answer is a single digit 0–9
understanding: We want the repeated digit-sum (digital root) of the number formed by writing `n` out `k` times. Writing it out is impossible (up to 10¹⁰ digits), but it's unnecessary: the digit-sum of `k` copies of `n` is simply `k · digitSum(n)`. So we seed the reduction with that single product and then collapse to one digit. The final value is the digital root, which has a closed form modulo 9.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we actually need to build the string repeated k times?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — and we mustn't. The digit-sum of k concatenated copies equals k times the digit-sum of one copy, so we collapse it without ever forming p.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n be larger than a 64-bit integer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — up to 10⁵ digits. Treat n as a string and sum its digit characters; never parse it as a numeric type.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What is the relationship to the digital root?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The super digit is exactly the digital root. For any m > 0 it equals 1 + (m − 1) mod 9, which lets you finish in O(1) after computing the seed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the answer be 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only if the seed is 0 (all digits zero). Otherwise the digital root is between 1 and 9.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Recursive Digit Sum is the 'collapse the repetition, then digital root' branch — never expand p.

approaches.name: Brute Reduction — Sum Digits of the Seed Repeatedly
approaches.whenToMention: The clear, safe baseline once you've made the digitSum·k collapse — reduce by literal digit-summing.
hints: First collapse the k copies: `seed = digitSum(n) · k`. This avoids building the giant number.
Now reduce `seed` to one digit by the literal definition: while it has more than one digit, replace it with the sum of its digits.
Return the final single digit. The reduction loop runs only a few times because each pass shrinks the number drastically.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Computing digitSum(n) scans the |n| characters once → O(|n|). The seed is at most 9·|n|·k, whose digit count is O(log(seed)); each reduction pass cuts it roughly to its digit-sum, converging in a handful of iterations. Constant extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Honor the recursive definition directly, but on the collapsed seed rather than the impossible full number.

**Collapse first.** The number `p` is `n` written `k` times. Its digit-sum is just every digit of `n` summed, `k` times over — i.e. `k · digitSum(n)`. So set `seed = digitSum(n) * k`. We've replaced an O(|n|·k)-length number with a single integer at most `9 · |n| · k`.

**Reduce literally.** Now apply the definition: while `seed` has more than one digit, sum its digits and repeat. For `n = "148", k = 3`: `digitSum = 13`, `seed = 39`, then `3 + 9 = 12`, then `1 + 2 = 3`. Return 3.

**Why this is enough.** Each reduction step replaces a number with its digit-sum, which is dramatically smaller (a 10-digit number drops to at most 90, then to at most 17, then to one digit), so the loop terminates in two or three passes regardless of input size. It's the straightforward, obviously-correct method; the closed-form below just collapses those last passes into one arithmetic expression.
approaches.insight: The only trick needed for correctness is the digitSum·k collapse — after that, the recursive definition is trivially cheap because digit-summing shrinks a number to roughly its logarithm each pass.

dryRun.intro: Collapse to a seed, then reduce by summing digits until one remains.

code.python:
def super_digit(n: str, k: int) -> int:
    seed = sum(int(d) for d in n) * k          # k copies → multiply once
    while seed >= 10:                           # reduce to a single digit
        seed = sum(int(d) for d in str(seed))
    return seed

approaches.name: Digital Root — Closed Form (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The tight answer. After seeding with digitSum(n)·k, finish in O(1) with `1 + (seed − 1) mod 9`.
hints: Repeated digit-summing in base 10 is the digital root, and the digital root of m is congruent to m modulo 9.
The clean formula for m > 0 is `1 + (m − 1) mod 9` — it maps multiples of 9 to 9 (not 0) and everything else to its remainder.
Seed with `m = digitSum(n) · k`, then return `0 if m == 0 else 1 + (m − 1) % 9`. No reduction loop needed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Summing the |n| digits is O(|n|); the multiply and the modulo are O(1). So the whole computation is O(|n|) time and O(1) space, independent of k.
approaches.explanation:
Replace the reduction loop with the arithmetic identity behind it.

**Why digit-summing = mod 9.** A number and the sum of its digits leave the same remainder modulo 9, because `10 ≡ 1 (mod 9)`, so `d_i · 10^i ≡ d_i (mod 9)`. Repeatedly digit-summing therefore preserves the value mod 9 and ends at the single digit congruent to it — that single digit is the **digital root**.

**The off-by-one fix.** Naively the digital root looks like `m mod 9`, but that maps multiples of 9 to `0`, whereas the true digital root of, say, 18 is `9`. The clean closed form `1 + (m − 1) mod 9` handles this: for `m = 18`, `1 + 17 mod 9 = 1 + 8 = 9`; for `m = 39`, `1 + 38 mod 9 = 1 + 2 = 3`. The only special case is `m = 0`, whose digital root is `0`.

**Apply to our seed.** As before, `m = digitSum(n) · k` (the k-copy collapse). Then the answer is `0 if m == 0 else 1 + (m − 1) % 9`. For `n = "148", k = 3`: `m = 13·3 = 39`, answer `1 + 38 % 9 = 1 + 2 = 3`. For `n = "9875", k = 4`: `m = 29·4 = 116`, `1 + 115 % 9 = 1 + 7 = 8`.

**Why prefer it.** It removes the reduction loop entirely, makes the divisibility-by-9 structure explicit, and is the canonical 'cast out nines' insight an interviewer is hoping you'll surface. The only real work is the single O(|n|) pass to compute `digitSum(n)`.
approaches.insight: Repeated digit-sum is a thin disguise for 'value mod 9'. The digital root `1 + (m−1) mod 9` is the same identity that powers the casting-out-nines arithmetic check — once you see it, any 'reduce to one digit' problem is O(1) after the digit-sum.

dryRun.intro: Seed with digitSum·k, then apply the digital-root closed form — no loop.

Closed-form digital root, O(1) after the digit-sum.

diagrams.title: Why digit-sum ≡ value mod 9
diagrams.caption: Since 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), each digit contributes itself mod 9 — repeated summing lands on the digital root.

edgeCases.behavior: digitSum = 0, m = 0 → returns 0. The all-zero guard.
m = 9 → 1 + (9−1)%9 = 1 + 8 = 9. Multiples of 9 map to 9, not 0.

pitfalls: Using `m % 9` directly — gives 0 for multiples of 9 instead of 9.
Forgetting the m == 0 guard, which would return 1 instead of 0.
Overflowing a 32-bit int for the seed — multiply into a long.

commonMistakes: Constructing the string n repeated k times, blowing up memory.
Reading n as a numeric integer when it can be up to 10⁵ digits long.
Using m % 9 for the digital root, which wrongly returns 0 for multiples of 9.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Building the repeated string
commonMistakesDetailed.why: n repeated k times can be 10¹⁰ characters — impossible to store. The digit-sum of k copies is just k times the digit-sum of one copy.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
p = n * k                       # up to 10^10 chars — memory blow-up
seed = sum(int(d) for d in p)
commonMistakesDetailed.good: seed = sum(int(d) for d in n) * k   # collapse without expanding

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong digital-root formula
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `m % 9` returns 0 for any multiple of 9, but the digital root of 18 is 9. Use `1 + (m − 1) % 9` for m > 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the seed
commonMistakesDetailed.why: digitSum(n)·k can reach 9·10⁵·10⁵ ≈ 9·10¹⁰, which overflows a 32-bit int. Use a 64-bit type.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int seed = digitSum * k;        // overflows for large n, k

patternNote: Digital-root reasoning: repeated digit-summing in base 10 preserves value mod 9, so the answer is `1 + (m−1) mod 9`. The k-fold repetition collapses to `digitSum(n)·k`, avoiding any big-number construction. This 'casting out nines' idea recurs wherever digits are summed to a fixed point.
